learningJourney.title: What is Sliding Window Maximum

explanation.foundation:
Pruning dominated candidates with a monotonic deque
When a window slides right by one element `nums[i]`, any older element `nums[j]` (`j < i`) inside the window that satisfies `nums[j] <= nums[i]` is **permanently dominated**: `nums[i]` is both larger (or equal) and will expire *later* than `nums[j]`. Therefore, `nums[j]` can never be the maximum of the current window or any future window. By popping all dominated elements from the back of a double-ended queue (`deque`) before appending `i`, the deque remains strictly decreasing in value and strictly increasing in index.
explanation.core:
**Core Pillars:**
- Store **indices** in the deque rather than raw values so you can check window expiration in $O(1)$ via `deque[0] <= i - k`.
- Maintain the monotonic decreasing invariant: before pushing index `i`, pop all back indices `j` where `nums[j] <= nums[i]` because `j` is both smaller and older, so it can never be the max of any future window.
- Amortized $O(1)$ per step: every index enters the back of the deque once and leaves either the front (expired) or back (dominated) at most once, yielding `<= 2n` deque operations total.
- The front of the deque (`nums[deque[0]]`) is always the exact maximum of the current window once `i >= k - 1`.
- A two-pass prefix/suffix block-max algorithm also achieves $O(n)$ time with $O(n)$ space and zero deque pointer chasing, ideal for SIMD/GPU batch arrays.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Sliding Window Maximum (and what fails without it)

explanation.foundation: Real-time stream processors (Apache Flink, Kafka Streams), network anomaly detectors, and financial tick engines continuously compute rolling peak CPU, peak latency, or max bid price over trailing `k`-event or `W`-second windows. At 100,000 events/sec with `k = 10,000`, an $O(n \cdot k)$ rescan executes $10^9$ comparisons per second and collapses, whereas a monotonic deque processes each event in amortized $O(1)$ time with predictable tail latency.
explanation.core:
**Common Pitfalls:**
- Using `list.pop(0)` in Python instead of `collections.deque.popleft()`, silently degrading the algorithm from $O(n)$ to $O(n \cdot k)$.
- Forgetting to check `i >= k - 1` before appending `nums[deque[0]]` to the result array, emitting partial-window maxima for the first `k - 1` elements.
- Evicting from the front *after* reading the maximum instead of *before* (or right after pushing `i`), returning an expired element.

learningJourney.title: How Sliding Window Maximum works under the hood & reference implementation

explanation.core:
Why the nested `while` loop is still $O(n)$
Although the algorithm places a `while` loop inside a `for` loop (`while dq and nums[dq[-1]] <= nums[i]: dq.pop()`), the total number of `pop()` operations across the *entire* run cannot exceed `n`, because each of the `n` indices is pushed onto `dq` exactly once. Combined with at most `n` `popleft()` operations, total deque work is bounded by `2n`—giving strict $O(n)$ worst-case time. Auxiliary space is bounded by $O(k)$ because `popleft()` ensures `dq` never spans more than `k` indices.
explanation.deepDive:
Trade-offs across sliding-window maximum techniques
| Approach | Time Complexity | Space Complexity | Streaming? | Best Use Case |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Monotonic Deque** | $O(n)$ | $O(k)$ | Yes | Standard online & interview optimal solution |
| **Max-Heap (Lazy Delete)** | $O(n \log n)$ worst | $O(n)$ worst | Yes | Multi-order queries or out-of-order deletions |
| **Two-Pass Block DP** | $O(n)$ | $O(n)$ | No (needs `n`) | Vectorized / SIMD offline array processing |
| **Segment Tree / Sparse Table** | $O(n \log n)$ | $O(n)$ / $O(n \log n)$ | No | Arbitrary variable-length `[L, R]` queries |
| **Brute Force Scan** | $O(n \cdot k)$ | $O(1)$ | Yes | Tiny windows (`k <= 8`) with zero allocation |

learningJourney.title: Production architecture & hardening for Sliding Window Maximum

explanation.foundation:
Bugs that break correctness or complexity
1. **ArrayDeque / List Front-Pop Penalty:** Using `ArrayList.remove(0)` in Java or `list.pop(0)` in Python shifts $O(k)$ elements on every eviction, turning $O(n)$ into $O(n \cdot k)$.
2. **Time-Based Window Skew:** In real-world streaming (e.g., max CPU in the last 60 seconds), the window size is measured in timestamps (`ts[i] - ts[dq[0]] >= 60_000`) rather than fixed index count `k`. Confusing count-based and time-based eviction breaks bursty streams.
3. **Integer Overflow in Comparator:** In Java/C++, subtracting `nums[dq.peekLast()] - nums[i]` overflows on `Integer.MIN_VALUE`; always use direct `<` / `<=` comparisons.
explanation.core:
Implementation & verification checklist
- [ ] **Store indices (or `(ts, val)`):** Never store raw values alone in the deque.
- [ ] **Evict before or right after window check:** Use `dq[0] <= i - k` for 0-indexed fixed windows of size `k`.
- [ ] **Use $O(1)$ double-ended queue:** `collections.deque` (Python) or `ArrayDeque` / primitive ring buffer (Java).
- [ ] **Verify `<=` vs `<`:** Use `<=` to keep the deque minimal; switch to `<` only if duplicates/earliest-index ties matter.
- [ ] **Handle boundary inputs:** Test `n == 0`, `k == 1`, `k == n`, strictly increasing, strictly decreasing, and all-equal arrays.
- [ ] **Emit only full windows:** Append to result only when `i >= k - 1`.

learningJourney.explanation:
## Pruning dominated candidates with a monotonic deque
When a window slides right by one element `nums[i]`, any older element `nums[j]` (`j < i`) inside the window that satisfies `nums[j] <= nums[i]` is **permanently dominated**: `nums[i]` is both larger (or equal) and will expire *later* than `nums[j]`. Therefore, `nums[j]` can never be the maximum of the current window or any future window. By popping all dominated elements from the back of a double-ended queue (`deque`) before appending `i`, the deque remains strictly decreasing in value and strictly increasing in index.

**Core Pillars:**
- Store **indices** in the deque rather than raw values so you can check window expiration in $O(1)$ via `deque[0] <= i - k`.
- Maintain the monotonic decreasing invariant: before pushing index `i`, pop all back indices `j` where `nums[j] <= nums[i]` because `j` is both smaller and older, so it can never be the max of any future window.
- Amortized $O(1)$ per step: every index enters the back of the deque once and leaves either the front (expired) or back (dominated) at most once, yielding `<= 2n` deque operations total.
- The front of the deque (`nums[deque[0]]`) is always the exact maximum of the current window once `i >= k - 1`.
- A two-pass prefix/suffix block-max algorithm also achieves $O(n)$ time with $O(n)$ space and zero deque pointer chasing, ideal for SIMD/GPU batch arrays.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Sliding Window Maximum (and what fails without it)
learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Sliding Window Maximum under real concurrency or scale.
learningJourney.explanation:
Real-time stream processors (Apache Flink, Kafka Streams), network anomaly detectors, and financial tick engines continuously compute rolling peak CPU, peak latency, or max bid price over trailing `k`-event or `W`-second windows. At 100,000 events/sec with `k = 10,000`, an $O(n \cdot k)$ rescan executes $10^9$ comparisons per second and collapses, whereas a monotonic deque processes each event in amortized $O(1)$ time with predictable tail latency.

**Common Pitfalls:**
- Using `list.pop(0)` in Python instead of `collections.deque.popleft()`, silently degrading the algorithm from $O(n)$ to $O(n \cdot k)$.
- Forgetting to check `i >= k - 1` before appending `nums[deque[0]]` to the result array, emitting partial-window maxima for the first `k - 1` elements.
- Evicting from the front *after* reading the maximum instead of *before* (or right after pushing `i`), returning an expired element.

ideas.title: Failure Mode
ideas.description: Mitigation: Always store integer indices (or `(timestamp, value)` pairs for time-based windows) in the deque.

ideas.title: Failure Mode
ideas.description: Mitigation: For a 0-indexed window `[i - k + 1, i]`, evict while `deque[0] <= i - k` (equivalently `deque[0] < i - k + 1`).

ideas.title: Failure Mode
ideas.description: Mitigation: Use a monotonic deque (hard-capped at `k` elements) instead of a lazy-deletion heap.

learningJourney.title: Where Sliding Window Maximum is used (and where to avoid it)
learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.
learningJourney.explanation: Sliding Window Maximum delivers the highest leverage at well-defined architectural boundaries. Use it for fixed-size (`k`) or time-bounded rolling max/min queries over streaming or array data where $O(n)$ throughput is required.

learningJourney.title: How Sliding Window Maximum works under the hood & reference implementation
learningJourney.purpose: Operational control: configure bounds, failure handling, and safe production defaults.
learningJourney.explanation:
## Step-by-step trace on `nums = [1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7], k = 3`
Maintain `dq` (indices) and `out`:
- `i=0 (1)`: `dq=[0(1)]`
- `i=1 (3)`: `3 >= 1` -> pop `0`, push `1`. `dq=[1(3)]`
- `i=2 (-1)`: `-1 < 3` -> push `2`. `dq=[1(3), 2(-1)]`. Window `[0..2]` full -> `out=[3]`
- `i=3 (-3)`: `-3 < -1` -> push `3`. `dq=[1(3), 2(-1), 3(-3)]`. `out=[3, 3]`
- `i=4 (5)`: `dq[0]=1 <= 4-3` -> pop front `1`. Then `5` pops `3(-3)` and `2(-1)` from back. `dq=[4(5)]`. `out=[3, 3, 5]`
- `i=5 (3)`: push `5`. `dq=[4(5), 5(3)]`. `out=[3, 3, 5, 5]`
- `i=6 (6)`: `6` pops `5(3)` and `4(5)`. `dq=[6(6)]`. `out=[3, 3, 5, 5, 6]`
- `i=7 (7)`: `7` pops `6(6)`. `dq=[7(7)]`. `out=[3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]`.

## Why the nested `while` loop is still $O(n)$
Although the algorithm places a `while` loop inside a `for` loop (`while dq and nums[dq[-1]] <= nums[i]: dq.pop()`), the total number of `pop()` operations across the *entire* run cannot exceed `n`, because each of the `n` indices is pushed onto `dq` exactly once. Combined with at most `n` `popleft()` operations, total deque work is bounded by `2n`—giving strict $O(n)$ worst-case time. Auxiliary space is bounded by $O(k)$ because `popleft()` ensures `dq` never spans more than `k` indices.

## Trade-offs across sliding-window maximum techniques
| Approach | Time Complexity | Space Complexity | Streaming? | Best Use Case |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Monotonic Deque** | $O(n)$ | $O(k)$ | Yes | Standard online & interview optimal solution |
| **Max-Heap (Lazy Delete)** | $O(n \log n)$ worst | $O(n)$ worst | Yes | Multi-order queries or out-of-order deletions |
| **Two-Pass Block DP** | $O(n)$ | $O(n)$ | No (needs `n`) | Vectorized / SIMD offline array processing |
| **Segment Tree / Sparse Table** | $O(n \log n)$ | $O(n)$ / $O(n \log n)$ | No | Arbitrary variable-length `[L, R]` queries |
| **Brute Force Scan** | $O(n \cdot k)$ | $O(1)$ | Yes | Tiny windows (`k <= 8`) with zero allocation |

learningJourney.title: Production architecture & hardening for Sliding Window Maximum
learningJourney.purpose: Production architecture: see how the components compose end to end under real load.
learningJourney.explanation:
## Bugs that break correctness or complexity
1. **ArrayDeque / List Front-Pop Penalty:** Using `ArrayList.remove(0)` in Java or `list.pop(0)` in Python shifts $O(k)$ elements on every eviction, turning $O(n)$ into $O(n \cdot k)$.
2. **Time-Based Window Skew:** In real-world streaming (e.g., max CPU in the last 60 seconds), the window size is measured in timestamps (`ts[i] - ts[dq[0]] >= 60_000`) rather than fixed index count `k`. Confusing count-based and time-based eviction breaks bursty streams.
3. **Integer Overflow in Comparator:** In Java/C++, subtracting `nums[dq.peekLast()] - nums[i]` overflows on `Integer.MIN_VALUE`; always use direct `<` / `<=` comparisons.

## Implementation & verification checklist
- [ ] **Store indices (or `(ts, val)`):** Never store raw values alone in the deque.
- [ ] **Evict before or right after window check:** Use `dq[0] <= i - k` for 0-indexed fixed windows of size `k`.
- [ ] **Use $O(1)$ double-ended queue:** `collections.deque` (Python) or `ArrayDeque` / primitive ring buffer (Java).
- [ ] **Verify `<=` vs `<`:** Use `<=` to keep the deque minimal; switch to `<` only if duplicates/earliest-index ties matter.
- [ ] **Handle boundary inputs:** Test `n == 0`, `k == 1`, `k == n`, strictly increasing, strictly decreasing, and all-equal arrays.
- [ ] **Emit only full windows:** Append to result only when `i >= k - 1`.

Store indices—not values—in a monotonically decreasing deque, evicting out-of-window indices from the front and smaller values from the back to hit strict $O(n)$ time.

advanced.summary: Sliding Window Maximum computes the maximum element in every contiguous subarray of size `k` across a length-`n` sequence in optimal $O(n)$ time and $O(k)$ space. By maintaining a monotonically decreasing double-ended queue (`deque`) of array indices, each element is pushed and popped at most once, beating naive $O(nk)$ scans and $O(n \log k)$ max-heaps.
